abstract: Real-time long-video generation requires continuous output with consistent appearance and natural motion. Existing chunk-wise autoregressive methods face challenges in both generation efficiency and long-video quality: serialized denoising and history-cache refresh require two forward passes even with one-step denoising, and longer rollouts can degrade quality and cause camera drift. We propose Wave Forcing (WF), which co-designs generation, training, and execution for continuous video output with multi-step denoising. WF uses chunk-wise causal attention to access earlier, cleaner chunks before their denoising is complete, and distributes staggered denoising and cache-refresh stages across full-model replicas to achieve 1F1C: one output chunk per concurrent forward round after pipeline fill. To adapt the model to this continuous generation process, we develop a three-stage training procedure that successively introduces mixed-noise denoising, motion supervision, and causal adaptation using self-generated history. To execute this process efficiently, Wave Runtime (WaveRT) uses Wave Parallelism (WP) for early K/V delivery and communication–computation overlap, together with optimized kernels and pipelined VAE decoding. Experiments on Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B show that 5-step WF maintains overall quality comparable to Rolling Forcing while achieving higher Dynamic Degree on both short and long videos. Our system efficiency experiments show that 4-step WF achieves 147.6 DiT FPS and 134.8 end-to-end FPS on eight H200 GPUs, yielding $\mathbf{7.07\times}$ the single-GPU end-to-end throughput. In DiT-only tests with matched SageAttention+W8A8 backends, denoising steps, and GPU counts, WP delivers up to $\mathbf{2.53\times}$ the throughput of the faster of the Ulysses and Ring context-parallel baselines across six model scales (1.3B–14B).

sections.body: Chunk-wise autoregressive video methods denoise each chunk and then run an extra store pass, so even one-step denoising takes two forward passes. Wave Forcing (WF) lets later chunks condition on earlier, cleaner chunks before those finish denoising, and places denoising and store stages on separate full-model replicas. Wave Runtime (WaveRT) implements Wave Parallelism to deliver key-value data early. On Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B, 5-step WF scores VBench Total 81.64 against 81.15 for Rolling Forcing. Dynamic Degree rises from 51.39 to 94.44 on short videos and from 36.63 to 91.45 on 100-second videos. The 4-step system reaches 147.6 DiT FPS and 134.8 end-to-end FPS on eight H200 GPUs, a 7.07× end-to-end speedup over the 19.06-FPS single-GPU baseline. Residual output-path overhead remains visible.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Wave Forcing targets one chunk per forward round and reports 147.6 DiT FPS and 134.8 end-to-end FPS on eight H200 GPUs.

sections.body: Each chunk undergoes S history-conditioned denoising updates, from noise to a clean output. A store step is a full-model forward on that clean output. It keeps the layer-wise key-value cache and discards the prediction. Sequential generation therefore uses N = S + 1 forwards per chunk, labeled NF1C. In the wavefront view, a filled tick holds denoising inputs for stages 0 to S−1, each at a different chunk. Adding store gives a window of width at most S + 1, excluding anchor and history caches. With stage-owned replicas, this schedule permits one chunk per round after fill without changing the work done per chunk.
sections.heading: Preliminaries
sections.headline: Sequential chunk generation needs S denoising forwards plus one store forward, so even one-step denoising takes two passes.

sections.body: Wave Forcing keeps full attention inside each chunk. Across chunks, a query slot attends to its own slot and to all cleaner predecessor slots, but never to later, noisier ones. This removes the reverse refinement used by Rolling Forcing. Because the causal mask changes the conditioning the pretrained model learned, the method adds three training stages. Stage 1 applies mixed-noise initialization with Rolling Forcing or Self Forcing rollouts. Stage 2 applies off-policy distribution matching distillation on re-noised teacher chunks, with a perceptual loss. Stage 3 samples Rolling Forcing, Wave Forcing, or Self Forcing rollouts with equal probability. The text states that without post-training, short-video Quality and Dynamic Degree fall in the authors' evaluation.
sections.heading: Wave Forcing
sections.headline: Chunk-wise causal attention lets newer chunks read earlier, cleaner chunks before those finish denoising.

sections.body: Each denoising stage and the store stage owns a full-model GPU replica. Each rank passes its updated chunk to the next rank. Attention waits for store and every legal cleaner rank to supply key-value data, while local projections proceed. Wave Runtime writes key-value data after projection and rotary position encoding, then checks readiness just before attention. The exposed wait on each edge is the larger of zero and its delivery cost minus its available lead time. Paged delivery writes remote segments directly into final attention slots, avoiding per-layer concatenation. Quantized key-value payloads reduce transfer size, but faster local operators can alter producer-consumer progress. The text notes that logical key-value fan-out remains quadratic in the number of stages.
sections.heading: Wave Runtime
sections.headline: Wave Runtime publishes key-value data early from stage-owned replicas, overlapping transfers with computation to cut waits.

sections.body: Table 1 compares 4-step and 5-step Wave Forcing on Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B with Rolling Forcing and Causal Forcing. On short videos, the 5-step model reaches VBench Total 81.64 and Quality 84.40, against 81.15 and 83.77 for Rolling Forcing. On 100-second videos, Dynamic Degree is 91.45 against 36.63. Subject Preservation is 97.10 against 92.75, and Camera Drift is 0.37 against 0.17. Causal Forcing reaches VBench-Long Dynamic Degree 96.61, but its Subject Preservation is 71.11 and its Camera Drift is 11.14. In Table 2, removing off-policy training lowers Quality to 76.68. In system tests, 4-step WaveRT reaches 134.81 E2E FPS on eight GPUs, 7.07× the single-GPU baseline.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: Five-step Wave Forcing scores 81.64 VBench Total against 81.15 for Rolling Forcing, with higher motion and subject retention.

sections.body: Prior streaming methods train on self-generated histories, restore gradient supervision for historical key-value data, or distill to few steps. Blockwise diffusion has appeared in language modeling and in vision-language-action models, where blocks are denoised at heterogeneous noise levels. Ulysses and Ring partition individual forward passes. Wave Parallelism instead schedules chunk-stage tasks on full-model replicas. The authors state that high Quality and Dynamic Degree can coexist with subject loss and camera drift, so they supplement benchmark scores with stability diagnostics. These lines frame the joint design of causal conditioning, training, and execution.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Related work spans streaming video training, blockwise diffusion in language and robotics, and parallel execution baselines.

sections.body: The stability diagnostics use a 100-prompt, subject-focused MovieGen subset and tracking heuristics. Their threshold sensitivity and agreement with human judgment remain untested. Aggregate timings do not isolate VAE compute, transfers, queueing, or backpressure. At four steps, the 1.3B BF16 configuration reaches 147.58 DiT FPS and 134.81 E2E FPS. At five steps it reaches 104.82 and 96.46. For 14B BF16, the gap narrows to 28.74 versus 28.64 DiT/E2E FPS. The advantage over context parallelism narrows for larger models, and stage parallelism is bounded by the step count. Online condition changes and serving latency are not evaluated.
sections.heading: Limitations
sections.headline: Subject and drift diagnostics rely on a 100-prompt subset, and output-path decoding capacity remains unresolved.

sections.body: Planned work profiles decoder stages, transfers, queues, and backpressure to guide allocation between denoising and VAE GPUs. It also studies finer-grained or hybrid parallelism combined with context parallelism. Serving research will address admission control, batching, and fairness for concurrent WF streams. Startup delay, output jitter, and playback stalls will be measured alongside throughput. Mid-generation prompt updates require deciding which active chunks receive each update and how affected state is refreshed. Camera and action control would extend the work toward interactive world models. The text describes all of these as prospective extensions that have not been evaluated.
sections.heading: Future Work
sections.headline: Future work targets end-to-end profiling, mid-generation prompt changes, and interactive world models, none yet evaluated.

sections.body: The conclusion summarizes Wave Forcing in three parts. Causal wavefront context uses cleaner intermediate states of preceding chunks. Three-stage training adapts the model to mixed-noise contexts and self-generated histories. A replica pipeline lets WaveRT overlap key-value delivery with computation. The authors report that WF improves motion while maintaining overall generation quality, and that it achieves high-throughput streaming video generation. They conclude that cross-chunk parallelism can translate into practical efficiency gains. The section restates earlier results and adds no new measurements.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: Jointly designing context, training, and execution yields one chunk per forward round after fill with comparable overall quality.

sections.body: The statement says AI assistants were used for conceptual framing and manuscript organization. They also supported discussion of methodology and systems analogies, interpretation of implementation and experimental evidence, translation and editing of text, and development and revision of figures. The statement says this assistance does not constitute independent verification of the reported results. The authors state that they remain responsible for the paper's claims, citations, and disclosures.
sections.heading: AI Use Statement
sections.headline: AI assistants supported framing, organization, editing, and figure work, and the authors remain responsible for the claims.

sections.body: Appendix A gives the 4-step schedule as `[1000,750,500,250]` and the 5-step schedule as `[1000,800,600,400,200]`, before timestep warping with shift factor 5. It also gives student and fake-score learning rates of 1.5×10^-6 and 4×10^-7. Appendix B describes process ownership, key-value publication, paged buffers, the round schedule, and streaming VAE partitioning. It includes Proposition 1, which states that dependency-respecting asynchronous execution produces the same latent sequence as synchronized execution. Appendices C and D cover evaluation and repetition. Table 11 lists six model configurations. Appendix E develops extensions that have not been evaluated with Wave Forcing.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists training schedules and loss details, runtime buffer and cache semantics, the same-graph proof, parameter configurations, and extended future work.
